subjective.question: Define a topology and a topological space. Give one example.
subjective.answer: Let X be a nonempty set. A collection τ of subsets of X is called a topology on X if it satisfies the following three axioms: (i) ∅ ∈ τ and X ∈ τ. (ii) The union of any number of members of τ belongs to τ. (iii) The intersection of any finite number of members of τ belongs to τ. The pair (X, τ) is then called a topological space, and the members of τ are called open sets (or τ-open sets). Example: For X = {a, b, c}, the collection τ = {∅, {a}, {a, b}, X} is a topology on X, because ∅ and X are in τ, every union of its members is again in τ, and every finite intersection of its members is again in τ.

subjective.question: Define open set and closed set in a topological space. Show that ∅ and X are
subjective.answer: always both open and closed. Let (X, τ) be a topological space. A subset U of X is called open if U ∈ τ. A subset F of X is called closed if its complement X − F is open, i.e. X − F ∈ τ. By the first axiom of a topology, ∅ and X are open. The complement of ∅ is X, which is open, so ∅ is closed; the complement of X is ∅, which is open, so X is closed. Hence ∅ and X are both open and closed (clopen) in every topological space.

subjective.question: Give an example to show that the union of two topologies on a set need not
subjective.answer: be a topology. Let X = {a, b, c} and consider the two topologies T_1 = {∅, {a}, X} and T_2 = {∅, {b}, X}. Their union is T_1 ∪ T_2 = {∅, {a}, {b}, X}. But {a} ∪ {b} = {a, b} ∉ T_1 ∪ T_2, so the union fails the union axiom and is not a topology on X. Hence the union of two topologies need not be a topology. (In contrast, the intersection of any collection of topologies on X is always a topology on X.)

subjective.question: Define the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology. Which of them is
subjective.answer: the finest and which is the coarsest topology on a set? Discrete topology: The topology on a set X consisting of all subsets of X, i.e. τ = P(X) (the power set of X), is called the discrete topology, and (X, P(X)) is called a discrete space. Every subset of a discrete space is open (and also closed). Indiscrete topology: The topology on X consisting only of ∅ and X, i.e. τ = {∅, X}, is called the indiscrete (or trivial) topology. The discrete topology is the largest (finest) topology that can be defined on X, because it contains every possible open set; the indiscrete topology is the smallest (coarsest) topology on X, because every topology on X must contain ∅ and X.

subjective.question: Define the cofinite (finite complement) topology on a set X.
subjective.answer: The cofinite topology on a set X is the collection τ of all subsets U of X such that either U = ∅ or the complement X − U is finite: τ = {U ⊆ X : U = ∅ or X − U is finite}. It is also called the finite complement topology. The nonempty open sets are exactly the subsets whose complements are finite. If X itself is finite, the cofinite topology on X is the discrete topology.

subjective.question: Define a limit point (accumulation point) of a set and the derived set of a set.
subjective.answer: Let (X, τ) be a topological space and A ⊆ X. A point x ∈ X is called a limit point (or accumulation point) of A if every open set U containing x contains a point of A different from x, i.e. U ∩ (A − {x}) ≠ ∅ for every open U with x ∈ U. The derived set of A, denoted by A′ (or A^d), is the set of all limit points of A: A′ = {x ∈ X : x is a limit point of A}. The derived set of A may or may not be a subset of A; for example, in ℝ with the usual topology, the derived set of (0, 3) is [0, 3]. In a discrete space the derived set of every set is empty.

subjective.question: Define the closure of a set. Prove that the closure of the empty set is empty,
subjective.answer: i.e. ∅̄ = ∅. The closure of a subset A of a topological space X, denoted by Ā, is the intersection of all closed subsets of X that contain A. It is the smallest closed subset of X containing A, and A is closed if and only if Ā = A. Proof that ∅̄ = ∅: The empty set ∅ is itself a closed set (its complement X is open), and ∅ ⊆ ∅. Hence ∅ is the smallest closed set containing ∅, so by definition the closure of ∅ is ∅ itself: ∅̄ = ∅.

subjective.question: In a topological space, prove that X̄ = X. (2 Marks)
subjective.answer: The closure X̄ of X is the intersection of all closed subsets of X containing X. The only subset of X that contains X is X itself, and X is a closed set (its complement ∅ is open). Hence the intersection reduces to X alone, so X̄ = X.

subjective.question: Let (X, T) be an indiscrete topological space and A a nonempty subset of X.
subjective.answer: Find the closure of A, and determine which subsets of X are dense in X. In the indiscrete space the only open sets are ∅ and X, so the only closed sets are also ∅ and X. The closure of A is the smallest closed set containing A. Since A ≠ ∅, the set ∅ cannot contain A, so the smallest closed set containing A is X itself. Hence Ā = X for every nonempty A ⊆ X. A set A is dense in X if and only if Ā = X. Therefore in an indiscrete space every nonempty subset is dense in X (and ∅ is not dense, since ∅̄ = ∅ ≠ X).

subjective.question: Show that for a subset A of a topological space X, if the derived set of A is
subjective.answer: contained in A (A′ ⊆ A), then A is closed. (5 Marks) Recall the standard identity Ā = A ∪ A′, i.e. the closure of A is the union of A and its derived set. Given A′ ⊆ A, we have A ∪ A′ = A. Therefore Ā = A ∪ A′ = A. A set is closed if and only if it is equal to its closure. Since Ā = A, the set A is closed. ∎

subjective.question: Define a dense subset of a topological space. Show that ℚ is dense in ℝ with
subjective.answer: the usual topology. A subset A of a topological space X is called dense in X if Ā = X, i.e. the closure of A is the whole space; equivalently, every nonempty open set of X meets A. Between any two real numbers there lies a rational number. Hence every open interval (a, b) ⊆ ℝ contains a rational number, so every point of ℝ is either in ℚ or a limit point of ℚ. Therefore ℚ̄ = ℝ, i.e. ℚ is dense in ℝ. (In contrast, ℕ is not dense in ℝ, because e.g. the open interval (3/2, 7/4) contains no natural number, so ℕ̄ = ℕ ≠ ℝ.)

subjective.question: Construct a topological space in which the open sets are identical to the
subjective.answer: closed sets. (3 Marks) Take any nonempty set X with the discrete topology τ = P(X). Every subset of X is open. Let A ⊆ X be any set; its complement X − A is also a subset of X, hence is open, which means A is closed. Thus every subset of X is both open and closed, so the family of open sets and the family of closed sets are both equal to P(X) — they are identical. For example, on X = {a, b} the discrete topology {∅, {a}, {b}, X} has closed sets ∅, {b}, {a}, X — exactly the same family.

subjective.question: Define the interior, the exterior and the boundary of a set A in a topological
subjective.answer: space. Let A be a subset of a topological space X. Interior of A: Int(A) (or A°) is the union of all open subsets of X that are contained in A. It is the largest open set contained in A, and a point of Int(A) is called an interior point of A. Exterior of A: Ext(A) is the interior of the complement of A, i.e. Ext(A) = Int(X − A). It is the largest open set contained in X − A, and its points are called exterior points of A. Boundary of A: bd(A) is the set of points x ∈ X such that every open set containing x meets both A and X − A. Equivalently, bd(A) = Ā ∩ (X − A)̄. Its points are called boundary (frontier) points of A. Every point of X belongs to exactly one of Int(A), bd(A) and Ext(A); that is, X = Int(A) ∪ bd(A) ∪ Ext(A), a disjoint union.

subjective.question: If A is a subset of a topological space X, explain why Ext(A) ∩ Int(A) = ∅.
subjective.answer: By definition, Int(A) is the union of all open sets contained in A, so Int(A) ⊆ A. Also Ext(A) = Int(X − A) ⊆ X − A. Thus Int(A) lies entirely inside A while Ext(A) lies entirely inside the complement of A. Since A and X − A are disjoint, no point can belong to both Int(A) and Ext(A). Hence Ext(A) ∩ Int(A) = ∅.

subjective.question: Prove that Ext(A^c) = Int(A), where A^c denotes the complement of A.
subjective.answer: By definition, the exterior of any set B is the interior of its complement: Ext(B) = Int(B^c). Applying this to B = A^c gives Ext(A^c) = Int((A^c)^c) = Int(A), because the complement of the complement of A is A itself. Hence Ext(A^c) = Int(A). ∎

subjective.question: Prove that (Int(A) ∪ bd(A))^c = Ext(A).
subjective.answer: Every point of X is of exactly one of the three types: an interior point of A, a boundary point of A, or an exterior point of A. Hence X is the disjoint union X = Int(A) ∪ bd(A) ∪ Ext(A). Removing the part Int(A) ∪ bd(A) from X leaves exactly Ext(A); in other words, the complement of Int(A) ∪ bd(A) in X is Ext(A): (Int(A) ∪ bd(A))^c = Ext(A). ∎

subjective.question: Define a neighborhood of a point in a topological space, and state two
subjective.answer: properties of the neighborhood system of a point. Let (X, τ) be a topological space and p ∈ X. A subset N of X is called a neighborhood of p if there exists an open set U such that p ∈ U ⊆ N. If N itself is open, it is called an open neighborhood of p. The class of all neighborhoods of p is called the neighborhood system of p, denoted by N_p. Two properties of N_p: (i) N_p is nonempty: X itself is a neighborhood of p, so p has at least one neighborhood; in fact every neighborhood of p contains p. (ii) N_p is closed under finite intersections: if N_1 and N_2 are neighborhoods of p, then N_1 ∩ N_2 is also a neighborhood of p. (Also, every superset of a neighborhood of p is a neighborhood of p.) A point p is an interior point of a set A if and only if A is a neighborhood of p.

subjective.question: Consider the topology T = {∅, {a}, {c, d}, {a, c, d}, {b, c, d, e}, X} on X =
subjective.answer: {a, b, c, d, e}. Determine the derived set of A = {a, b, c}. A point x is in the derived set A′ if every open set containing x meets A − {x} = {a, b, c} − {x}. • x = a: the open set {a} contains a, but {a} ∩ {b, c} = ∅. So a is not a limit point. • x = b: the open sets containing b are {b, c, d, e} and X; {b, c, d, e} ∩ {a, c} = {c} ≠ ∅ and X ∩ {a, c} ≠ ∅. So b is a limit point. • x = c: the open set {c, d} contains c, but {c, d} ∩ {a, b} = ∅. So c is not a limit point. • x = d: every open set containing d ({c, d}, {a, c, d}, {b, c, d, e}, X) contains c ∈ A. So d is a limit point. • x = e: the open sets containing e are {b, c, d, e} and X, and both meet A (in b and c). So e is a limit point. Hence the derived set of A is A′ = {b, d, e}.

subjective.question: Consider the topology T = {∅, {a}, {a, b}, {a, c, d}, {a, b, c}, X} on X = {a,
subjective.answer: b, c, d}. For the subset A = {a, b, c}, find the interior points, the exterior points and the boundary points of A. Interior points of A: a point x is an interior point if some open set containing x is contained in A. • a: {a} ⊆ A, so a is an interior point. • b: {a, b} ⊆ A, so b is an interior point. • c: the open set {a, b, c} = A contains c and is contained in A, so c is an interior point. • d: d ∉ A, so d is not an interior point. Hence Int(A) = {a, b, c} = A (indeed A itself is an open set). Exterior points of A: these are the interior points of A^c = {d}. The open sets containing d are {a, c, d} and X, and neither is contained in {d}. So A has no exterior points: Ext(A) = ∅. Boundary points of A: a point x is a boundary point if every open set containing x meets both A and A^c = {d}. • a: {a} ∩ A^c = ∅, so a is not a boundary point. Similarly b ({a, b} ∩ A^c = ∅) and c ({a, b, c} ∩ A^c = ∅) are not boundary points. • d: the open sets containing d, {a, c, d} and X, both meet A and A^c. So d is a boundary point. Hence bd(A) = {d}. (Check: Int(A) ∪ Ext(A) ∪ bd(A) = {a, b, c} ∪ ∅ ∪ {d} = X.)

subjective.question: Define the subspace (relative) topology on a subset of a topological space.
subjective.answer: What is a relatively open set? Let A be a nonempty subset of a topological space (X, T). The collection T_A = {V = U ∩ A : U ∈ T} of subsets of A is a topology on A, called the subspace topology (or relative topology) on A. The space (A, T_A) is called a subspace of (X, T). A subset V of A is called relatively open (open in A) if V ∈ T_A, i.e. if V = U ∩ A for some open set U of X. Example: in the subspace [0, 1] of ℝ with the usual topology, the set [0, 1/2) = (−1, 1/2) ∩ [0, 1] is relatively open, although it is not open in ℝ.

subjective.question: Define a basis for a topology. State the relation between a topology and its
subjective.answer: basis. Let (X, T) be a topological space. A subcollection B ⊆ T is called a basis (or base) for the topology T if for every U ∈ T and every x ∈ U there exists a member B ∈ B such that x ∈ B ⊆ U. Equivalently, every open set U ∈ T can be written as a union of members of B; one says that T is the topology generated by B. The members of B are called basis elements or basic open sets. Example: the collection of all open intervals (a, b) is a basis for the usual topology on ℝ, and the collection of all open disks is a basis for the usual topology on ℝ². A basis for the discrete topology on X is the collection of all singletons {{x} : x ∈ X}, and a basis for the indiscrete topology {∅, X} is simply {X}.

subjective.question: Prove that a function f : (X, T_X) → (Y, T_Y) is continuous if and only if the
subjective.answer: inverse image of every closed subset of Y under f is closed in X. (5 Marks) (⇒) Suppose f is continuous and let F be a closed subset of Y. Then Y − F is open in Y, so by continuity f⁻¹(Y − F) is open in X. But f⁻¹(Y − F) = X − f⁻¹(F), so X − f⁻¹(F) is open in X, which means f⁻¹(F) is closed in X. (⇐) Conversely, suppose the inverse image of every closed subset of Y is closed in X. Let U be an open subset of Y. Then Y − U is closed in Y, so by assumption f⁻¹(Y − U) is closed in X. But f⁻¹(Y − U) = X − f⁻¹(U), so X − f⁻¹(U) is closed, which means f⁻¹(U) is open in X. Hence the inverse image of every open subset of Y is open in X, i.e. f is continuous. ∎

subjective.question: Show that f : (X, T_X) → (Y, T_Y) is continuous if and only if the inverse
subjective.answer: image of each member of a basis B_Y for T_Y is an open subset of X. (3 Marks) (⇒) If f is continuous, then since every member of the basis B_Y is an open subset of Y, its inverse image under f is open in X by the definition of continuity. (⇐) Suppose f⁻¹(B) is open in X for every B ∈ B_Y. Let U be any open subset of Y. Since B_Y is a basis, U is a union of basis members: U = ∪_{i} B_i with B_i ∈ B_Y. Then f⁻¹(U) = f⁻¹(∪_{i} B_i) = ∪_{i} f⁻¹(B_i). Each f⁻¹(B_i) is open in X by assumption, and a union of open sets is open, so f⁻¹(U) is open in X. Hence f is continuous. ∎

subjective.question: Define continuity of a function at a point p ∈ X. (2 Marks)
subjective.answer: Let f : (X, T_X) → (Y, T_Y) be a function and p ∈ X. The function f is called continuous at the point p if for every open set V of Y containing f(p), there exists an open set U of X containing p such that f(U) ⊆ V; equivalently, the inverse image of every neighborhood of f(p) is a neighborhood of p. A function f is continuous on X if and only if it is continuous at every point p of X.

subjective.question: Define an open map and a homeomorphism. Show that there is no
subjective.answer: homeomorphism between the open interval (0, 1) and the closed interval [0, 1] of ℝ. (2 Marks) A map f : X → Y between topological spaces is called an open map if the image of every open subset of X is open in Y. A map f : X → Y is called a homeomorphism if f is bijective, f is continuous, and f⁻¹ is continuous. Two spaces between which a homeomorphism exists are called homeomorphic (topologically equivalent). No homeomorphism (0, 1) → [0, 1] exists: removing a point from a space is a topological property. In [0, 1], removing the endpoint 0 leaves (0, 1], which is still connected; in fact [0, 1] has points (its endpoints) whose removal leaves the space connected. But removing any point x from (0, 1) splits it into (0, x) ∪ (x, 1), a disconnected set. A homeomorphism would carry one situation to the other, which is impossible. Hence (0, 1) and [0, 1] are not homeomorphic.

subjective.question: Explain why an indiscrete space with more than one point is not metrizable.
subjective.answer: (2 Marks) Every metrizable space is a metric space for some metric, and every metric space is Hausdorff (T_2): any two distinct points can be separated by disjoint open balls. But in an indiscrete space X with at least two points, the only nonempty open set is X itself, so any two distinct points cannot be separated by disjoint open sets — the space is not Hausdorff. Since metrizable implies Hausdorff and the indiscrete space is not Hausdorff, it is not metrizable.
